flashcards.q: Name the four C4 levels and which one an interview wants.
flashcards.a: L1 Context (your system plus users and external systems, 5-8 boxes, no internals); L2 Container (separately deployable/runnable things with technology and communication, 8-15 boxes) which IS the interview diagram; L3 Component (major modules inside one container, 5-8 boxes) for the deep dive only; L4 Code (classes) which is effectively dead, never draw it.

flashcards.q: What is a C4 container, precisely?
flashcards.a: Anything separately deployable and runnable: a service, a single-page app, a mobile app, a database, a queue, an object-store bucket, a Lambda. Not the same as a Docker container: a sidecar is not a separate C4 container, and a database schema on a shared cluster is one even though it is not containerised.

flashcards.q: Which of the four diagram types answers which question?
flashcards.a: C4 container: what exists, what technology, where state lives, sync vs async. Sequence: order, latency budget decomposition, failure/degradation in time. Dataflow: transformation, volume, throughput ceiling, replay-safety. Deployment: what it runs on, blast radius per failure domain, RPO/RTO, source of truth vs derived index. None can answer another's question, which is why one big diagram always fails.

flashcards.q: What is the very first mark you make on a blank whiteboard?
flashcards.a: Not a box. Divide the space: ~20% left for requirements, NFR table, and numbers (never erased), ~55% middle for the container diagram, ~25% right kept empty for deep dives. Then place two anchors, client far left and primary datastore far right, so the architecture grows between them and you cannot run out of room.

flashcards.q: State the drawing order that keeps the narrative coherent.
flashcards.a: Two anchors, then the happy-path READ end to end without adding anything else, then the WRITE path below it from the same entry point, then the ASYNC path below a visible horizontal line, then a second pass to annotate numbers, then deep dives in the reserved right column. Narrate every transition out loud.

protocol/format, sync or async, payload size, rate or latency. Two are mandatory (protocol and sync/async). Example: HTTPS/JSON, sync, 6 KB, 15k rps. Solid line = sync, dashed = async, never changing within a diagram. Arrow direction means INITIATES, not data flow, and you state which convention you use.

flashcards.q: Why does sync versus async on an edge matter so much?
flashcards.a: Sync edges sum into the latency budget: a 200 ms p99 target across five sync hops gives each ~40 ms before processing. Async edges contribute nothing to the budget but each incurs a durability obligation instead: at-least-once delivery, an idempotent consumer, and a lag metric to alert on. Drawing them identically means the diagram answers neither question.

flashcards.q: List the six steps of the scale-annotation pass.
flashcards.a: 1) Rate on hot edges only. 2) Size on stateful boxes. 3) Replica count as a multiplier with failure-domain spread (x12, 3 AZ) instead of drawing 12 boxes. 4) Bottleneck double-boxed with its binding constraint. 5) Partition key on every sharded store. 6) A 'not drawn' text line listing omissions. Do this as a second pass; annotating while drawing slows you to a crawl.

flashcards.q: What do you leave out of an interview diagram, and how do you avoid looking forgetful?
flashcards.a: Authn/authz boxes (say OIDC at the gateway once), observability, CI/CD, DNS/TLS, secrets and config, internal load balancers, service mesh sidecars, individual replicas, and every cache layer at once. Write a one-line 'not drawn:' list, which converts each omission into a scoping decision. Rule: only draw what you can defend in depth, because every box invites a follow-up.

flashcards.q: Why cap a container diagram at 12-15 boxes?
flashcards.a: Human working memory is about 7 plus or minus 2 chunks, so past ~10 boxes the interviewer spends questions on comprehension instead of design. Recover legibility by grouping into 3-5 labelled regions (edge, read path, write path, async, storage) and collapsing replicas into multipliers.

flashcards.q: What must a sequence diagram include beyond the calls?
flashcards.a: Latency on every arrow, summed, with the dominant hop named (a sequence diagram without timings is a call graph with extra steps); the async escape drawn explicitly as a dashed line; and if there is time, one failure variant showing the degraded path (timeout, breaker opens, keyword-only fallback with a degraded flag).

flashcards.q: Five things a dataflow/pipeline diagram must include.
flashcards.a: Volume on every edge so the narrow stage is visible; the narrow stage marked with its burst policy (queue, shed, or drop); the dead-letter path with its expected failure rate; the idempotency key, because pipelines get replayed and where dedup happens is the most important detail; and the freshness SLO with the stage that owns it (usually the crawler interval, not the pipeline).

flashcards.q: What makes a deployment diagram real rather than decorative?
flashcards.a: Replica counts, instance types, and the anti-affinity guarantee that a shard's replicas land in different AZs (8 pods across 3 AZs can still put both replicas of a shard in one AZ); explicit RPO and RTO numbers; and a statement of which store is the source of truth versus a rebuildable derived index. Also: provision 1.5x so N-1 AZ capacity still sits at the target utilisation.

flashcards.q: What is wrong with a diagram full of cloud vendor icons?
flashcards.a: Icons encode the product name and nothing else: no responsibility, protocol, sync/async, throughput, or partition key, while looking authoritative. They also bias the design toward whatever has an icon, so candidates draw an SQS icon instead of deriving that they need a queue. A labelled box with a bracketed technology plus a labelled edge carries strictly more information in the same space.

flashcards.q: Which diagram do you reach for, given what the interviewer says?
flashcards.a: 'Design X' → C4 container (default). 'Walk me through what happens when...' or 'where does the latency go' → sequence. 'How does data get in / reindexing / freshness' → dataflow. 'What if an AZ dies / multi-region' → deployment. 'Tell me more about component Y' → C4 component in fresh space. 'Show me the schema' → not a diagram, write CREATE TABLE. 'Implement the queue' → not a diagram, write code.

flashcards.q: Why is labelling a forcing function rather than decoration?
flashcards.a: You cannot write 'sync, p99 12 ms' on an edge without having decided that hop's consistency and latency properties, and you cannot write a partition key without having decided the access pattern. Candidates who label discover their own gaps at minute 25 instead of the interviewer discovering them at minute 40. The labelling is where the thinking happens.

Mermaid is the repo default (rendered natively by GitHub/GitLab/Notion, strong sequence and flowchart support, weak C4). Structurizr DSL is right when C4 accuracy matters, because all levels derive from one model and cannot diverge. D2 has the best auto-layout for docs sites. PlantUML is the dated workhorse. Excalidraw/tldraw for canvas interviews. The real durable artefact is the ADR; the diagram indexes it.

flashcards.q: How do you keep an architecture diagram accurate over two years?
flashcards.a: Not by hand. Put it in the repo as Mermaid or Structurizr DSL so staleness surfaces in code review; generate the deployment view from Terraform or manifests so it derives from truth; and compare the declared container graph against the OpenTelemetry service graph to flag edges present in traffic but absent from the model. The last one is worth waiting for tooling on, because a homegrown version alerts on every health check and gets muted.
